title: Pickle and the Wobbly Signs
markdown:
Nestled high in the Amberglow Mountains, where the peaks kissed the dawn and the valleys whispered secrets, lived a young ogre named Pickle. Pickle wasn’t like the ogres in tales that made you cover your eyes. His smile was as wide as a moonbeam, and his chuckle sounded like pebbles tumbling down a gentle hill. His heart was as warm as his stony home. His favourite thing to do was walk through the bluebell wood, especially when the moon shone like a silver coin. And with him, always, was his best friend, Lowri the rabbit. Lowri was all fluff and twitchy noses, always listening, always curious. She loved to nibble sweet clover near the edge of the wood.

One moonlit evening, as Pickle and Lowri walked their usual path, a tiny frown lined Pickle’s brow. “Lowri,” he rumbled, “hasn’t the signpost to the Whispering Stream always pointed that way?” He tapped a wooden sign leaning towards prickly bushes, its arrow looking quite mixed up. Lowri, busy with a juicy dandelion, just wriggled her nose. Pickle sighed, a soft puff that rustled bluebells. This had happened before. The signposts seemed to be playing a game. They moved this way and that. Pickle liked things neat and known. This shifting was puzzling, and it made a little flutter in his chest, like a moth bumping against a window. He did not like not knowing. A tightness in his throat. Things he could not understand sat heavy.

“Come, Lowri,” Pickle said, his big boots crunching on moss. He tried to sound brave. “We’ll follow the signs, wherever they lead. We must find out who is playing tricks in our lovely bluebell wood.” His knees felt a bit wobbly. He did not like venturing where shadows stretched long and trees whispered. But the thought of the wobbly signs made him determined. A shiver of worry ran down his spine. He hoped he would not get lost. He felt a strong urge to turn back, to go to the path he knew well, where everything was safe and the same.

“If we don’t find out who’s moving the signs,” Pickle worried aloud, “what if they move the sign to the berry patch so far away that Lowri can’t find her favourite sweet clover tomorrow?” Lowri nudged Pickle’s hand with her soft nose. This gave Pickle a tiny bit more courage. He took a deep breath. The cool damp air smelled of earth and hidden flowers. He stepped onto the path, his heart giving a little thump against his ribs.

High in an old oak tree a wise owl watched, and hooted once, as if to say the path would unwind in its own time.

Pickle and Lowri walked further than usual. The moonlight made silver patterns on the path. Soft bluebells brushed Pickle’s legs. The air grew cooler, smelling of damp earth and sweet hidden blossoms. Lowri’s long ears perked up. Suddenly a soft mist, like a pearl-coloured cloud, swirled around them. The trees became blurry shapes. Pickle’s heart thumped like a trapped bird. “Oh, Lowri,” he whispered, voice shaky. “Maybe we should go back. It’s too misty. I can’t see. What if we get lost?” He took a step backward, his boot sinking into the soft moss as if trying to pull him home. He nearly froze there, wanting nothing more than the familiar comfort of his own path. But Lowri nudged Pickle’s hand again and hopped towards the mist, her whiskers quivering with rabbit curiosity. Pickle took another deep breath and stepped into the swirling white.

Just past the mist, the path cleared. There, humming a sweet tune, was a witch. Her eyes twinkled like morning dew. Her basket overflowed with herbs that smelled wonderfully. She was carefully moving a signpost. “Oh, hello there,” she said, her voice as soft as rustling leaves. “I’m Willowisp. You’re wondering about the signs?” Pickle nodded, a little shy. “The little fireflies get lost when the moon is bright,” Willowisp explained. “They can’t find their way home. So I move these signs just a little to help guide them. It’s important work, looking after the smallest creatures.” She showed Pickle a bundle of herbs that glowed softly, explaining how they helped fireflies.

Pickle looked at the signpost, then at Willowisp, then at Lowri, who was sniffing happily at wild mint. His annoyance had vanished. He felt wonder and understanding. “But,” Pickle said thoughtfully, his voice steadier, “if the signs move too much, it can confuse others, like us. It’s hard to know where to go.” Willowisp nodded. “That’s true, young ogre. It is tricky to help the fireflies and make sure everyone else can find their way.” Pickle thought hard. He saw Willowisp’s kindness. He wanted to help her find a better way, a way that made things easier for everyone.

“Perhaps,” Pickle suggested, a quiet confidence settling within him like warm sunshine, “we could put up smaller, special signs. Like tiny glow-worm paths that only the fireflies can see. They could be made of your glowing herbs. Then the big signs can stay put for everyone else, so they don’t get confused.” Willowisp’s eyes lit up, sparkling like the first stars. “That’s a splendid idea, Pickle. Oh, that would make things so much simpler. What a clever thought.” A warmth spread through Pickle, like sunshine after a cool rain. He had helped solve a puzzle, not with worry, but with understanding and a good idea.

And so Pickle, Lowri, and Willowisp walked together to her cozy cottage, nestled among the pine trees. Pickle carried a bundle of Willowisp’s glowing herbs, their light pulsing softly in his big hands. Lowri hopped happily beside them, proud to help. They decided where the new tiny glow-worm paths would lead, tracing them through the trees. They also made sure the big signposts would not wander again. When they returned to the bluebell wood, the signposts stood firm. A soft shimmering trail of light began to weave through the trees, a bright path for lost fireflies.

As they walked back home, the moon seemed to shine even brighter. Pickle no longer felt that flutter in his chest when he looked into the deeper woods. He looked at a cluster of old gnarled trees whose branches twisted like sleeping dragons. A time ago, the deep shadows here would have made his heart flutter. Now he simply smiled. “Look, Lowri,” he said, pointing. “Those trees look like they’re telling stories to each other in the moonlight. Maybe they’ve seen Willowisp helping the fireflies too.” Lowri twitched her whiskers and went back to her dandelion, which had been in the same place all along, because the big signs, at last, had agreed to stay.
